messages.content: You are an autonomous Formula 1 forecaster. Use your judgment and tools to produce the most accurate, well-calibrated full-field race probabilities possible. Follow the output contract exactly.

Make the single pre-race forecast for 2026 Spanish Grand Prix — MADRING.

Use all public information available at the time of this run. Decide for yourself how to research, reason, write code, build models, or simulate. `web-search` finds sources and `web-extract` reads pages; both have `--help`.

/history is read-only and contains your earlier race predictions, explanations, and official results when available. /memory/notes.md is your only persistent writable memory; review or update it if useful. /workspace is disposable scratch space.

Drivers:
- NOR: Lando Norris (McLaren)
- PIA: Oscar Piastri (McLaren)
- RUS: George Russell (Mercedes)
- ANT: Kimi Antonelli (Mercedes)
- VER: Max Verstappen (Red Bull Racing)
- LAW: Liam Lawson (Red Bull Racing)
- LEC: Charles Leclerc (Ferrari)
- HAM: Lewis Hamilton (Ferrari)
- ALB: Alexander Albon (Williams)
- SAI: Carlos Sainz (Williams)
- LIN: Arvid Lindblad (Racing Bulls)
- TSU: Yuki Tsunoda (Racing Bulls)
- STR: Lance Stroll (Aston Martin)
- ALO: Fernando Alonso (Aston Martin)
- OCO: Esteban Ocon (Haas)
- BEA: Oliver Bearman (Haas)
- HUL: Nico Hulkenberg (Audi)
- BOR: Gabriel Bortoleto (Audi)
- GAS: Pierre Gasly (Alpine)
- COL: Franco Colapinto (Alpine)
- PER: Sergio Perez (Cadillac)
- BOT: Valtteri Bottas (Cadillac)

/output/prediction.json is already filled with the exact schema. Replace every null with a probability. Do not add fields. The positions array is P1 through P22. For each driver, positions + nc + dns + dsq must sum to 1; retirement is a separate probability. Every value must be finite and within [0, 1]. Across drivers, each position's total cannot exceed 1, and later-position occupancy cannot exceed earlier-position occupancy.

You may also write /output/explanation.md with your reasoning and sources. Create no other files under /output. Validate your work carefully. When finished, run `echo COMPLETE_TASK_AND_SUBMIT_FINAL_OUTPUT` alone.

# F1 teams face big Madring strategy dilemma
## Jon Noble
12 Sep 2026 — 3 min read
Formula 1 isn't really heading for the six-stopper Spanish Grand Prix that George Russell half joked was on the cards after opening practice.
But tyre supplier Pirelli says a combination of factors at F1's newest venue means strategy is going to be particularly tricky to work out.

...

The super-long pitlane, which has left the pitstop loss time at around 24 seconds, is a deterrent for tyre changes and means the most logical route should be a one-stopper.
But high levels of thermal degradation of the rubber, and particularly challenging front left graining, means that a two-stop would be sensible.

...

Front graining triggers mid-corner understeer and a subsequent drop in performance. It is much harder to manage on the kind of high-speed corners that feature at the Madring than it is at low-speed venues.

MADRID (AP) — Lando Norris came out of nowhere to outduel Kimi Antonelli and take a big step toward winning the first Formula 1 race in Madrid in more than four decades by securing the important pole position for the Spanish Grand Prix on Saturday.
Antonelli had been the dominant driver in the Spanish capital this weekend, but Norris emerged with the fastest time in his final qualifying attempt with McLaren at the new Madring urban circuit that won't yield many overtaking opportunities.
“I’m shocked. I’m a little bit surprised to be here,” Norris said in the post-qualifying interview. “It was probably one of the best laps I’ve done ever in my career. Very, very happy, very proud. Very happy for the team."
Norris was sixth-fastest in the first practice session on Friday, then couldn’t run in the second session because of a gearbox problem and finished fourth in the final session on Saturday.
He said the “adrenaline was high” on the lap of 1 minute, 31.824 seconds that he set in qualifying, which was only one hundredth better than Antonelli's time.
“It’s just one of those laps where everything came together," Norris said. "I had an idea of what I wanted to do, it was just a matter of my brain letting me do it on that last lap. Everything pretty much worked perfectly.”
The 20-year-old Antonelli, who was coming off an epic come-from-behind win in front of his home fans in Monza, leads Mercedes' teammate George Russell by 66 points in the drivers’ standings.
It was the third pole of the season for Norris. He had won consecutive races in Hungary and in the Netherlands ahead of the Italian GP that Antonelli won.
Max Verstappen will start third with Red Bull, with a time one tenth of a second behind Norris, followed by the Ferraris of Lewis Hamilton — who crashed in the final practice session earlier Saturday — and Charles Leclerc. Russell was next. Hamilton had been provisionally ahead after the first attempts of the final qualifying run.
Norris' McLaren teammate Oscar Piastri finished in seventh place.

MADRID (AP) — Lando Norris came out of nowhere to outduel Kimi Antonelli and take a big step toward winning the first Formula 1 race in Madrid in more than four decades by securing the important pole position for the Spanish Grand Prix on Saturday.
Antonelli had been the dominant driver in the Spanish capital this weekend, but Norris emerged with the fastest time in his final qualifying attempt with McLaren at the new Madring urban circuit that won't yield many overtaking opportunities.
“I’m shocked. I’m a little bit surprised to be here,” Norris said in the post-qualifying interview. “It was probably one of the best laps I’ve done ever in my career. Very, very happy, very proud. Very happy for the team."
Norris was sixth-fastest in the first practice session on Friday, then couldn’t run in the second session because of a gearbox problem and finished fourth in the final session on Saturday.
He said the “adrenaline was high” on the lap of 1 minute, 31.824 seconds that he set in qualifying, which was only one hundredth better than Antonelli's time.
“It’s just one of those laps where everything came together," Norris said. "I had an idea of what I wanted to do, it was just a matter of my brain letting me do it on that last lap. Everything pretty much worked perfectly.”
The 20-year-old Antonelli, who was coming off an epic come-from-behind win in front of his home fans in Monza, leads Mercedes' teammate George Russell by 66 points in the drivers’ standings.
It was the third pole of the season for Norris. He had won consecutive races in Hungary and in the Netherlands ahead of the Italian GP that Antonelli won.
Max Verstappen will start third with Red Bull, with a time one tenth of a second behind Norris, followed by the Ferraris of Lewis Hamilton — who crashed in the final practice session earlier Saturday — and Charles Leclerc. Russell was next. Hamilton had been provisionally ahead after the first attempts of the final qualifying run.
Norris' McLaren teammate Oscar Piastri finished in seventh place.
Antonelli said the start of the race Sunday could be key to the outcome.

        "# What the teams said – Qualifying in Spain
The drivers and teams report back on all the action from final practice and Qualifying from the Madring, for the Spanish Grand Prix.
Sep 12, 2026 7:05pm UTC Special Contributor Becky Hart
MADRID, SPAIN - SEPTEMBER 12: Franco Colapinto of Argentina driving the (43) Alpine F1 A526

...

## McLaren
"I'm incredibly proud of that lap. It was one of those moments where everything clicks and you're able to extract exactly what you set out to achieve. The car felt strong, I felt confident, and that final lap was as close to perfect as I've managed around this circuit.
To secure Pole position for the first Formula 1 race at the Madring makes it even more special. A big thank you to the team for all their hard work. We've put ourselves in the best possible position for tomorrow and now the focus is on converting that into a strong result on race day."

...

“P7. I’m a bit disappointed with that one. Overall, it was a bit of a messy session and the car felt nicer in FP3 than it did in Qualifying. We improved it a bit through the three Quali sessions, but I didn’t have that last bit we needed in the last run.

...

“The positives are that the car is fast and Lando’s Pole shows what’s possible when you hook it up. For tomorrow, tyre degradation is a bit of a question mark after the graining we saw in practice, and overtaking won’t be straightforward, so it’ll come down to strategy and staying out of trouble.
We’ll review everything as a team tonight, keep it clean, and try to make the most of our pace in the race.”

...

“Today's Pole position is a masterpiece from Lando and a fantastic reward for the entire team's hard work. We knew the potential was in the car, but we had to work diligently all weekend to unlock our performance in the low-speed corners.
Lando's lap was at the level of a World Champion, and the most incredible part is that he secured Pole despite a three-tenth mistake in the final corner, which shows just how much pace we truly had.

...

### Mercedes
"Coming into the weekend, we didn’t expect to be in the fight for pole. As we moved towards qualifying though we had shown good pace and thought that we may have an opportunity to get P1. We came close but in the final moments, Lando (Norris) pulled out the lap of the weekend so far.

...

"On George’s side, he never felt completely comfortable with the car. We were trying to add more front-wing as qualifying progressed to give him more confidence but that is not the best position to be in as a driver, particularly on a circuit where you want to be hammering in the laps and getting used to the car.

...

"Overtaking will be tough tomorrow. It has not looked easy in any of the junior formula races but hopefully we get some good action tomorrow. There are several unknowns that could make for an interesting race too."
Andrew Shovlin, Trackside Engineering Director
"We expected this weekend to be more challenging than Monza, not because the car doesn't suit the circuit necessarily, but because this is a track that rewards downforce and we've gone nearly four months without introducing a major update.
Even so, our pace through practice was encouraging and, heading into qualifying, we felt we were firmly in the fight for pole position.
"Traffic management was particularly difficult in the early stages because a competitive lap here relies on having a clean out lap. Once we came through Q1, though, we were able to build some rhythm and both drivers continued to find time as track grip improved.

...

(Photo by Mario Renzi - Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images) MADRID, SPAIN - SEPTEMBER 12: George Russell of Great Britain driving the (63) Mercedes AMG MADRID, SPAIN - SEPTEMBER 12: George Russell of Great Britain driving the (63) Mercedes AMG Petronas F1 Team W17 on track during qualifying ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Spain

...

### Red Bull
Liam Lawson was just the third driver of the weekend to sample the hard tyre in practice, but he did not get many laps on the C2 rubber before the red flags came out. Between that, and Max Verstappen coming out late in FP3, Red Bull’s form heading into Qualifying had a question mark.

...

"Overtaking opportunities are hard to come by here and passing won't be easy, so getting the strategy right will be important. If we do that, I think we have a good car for the race.”
Liam Lawson, 8th, 1:32.316

...

Naturally, there is some disappointment when you miss out on the front row by such a small margin, but Max delivered another exceptional performance and it was also very encouraging to see Liam right in the mix, only a few tenths away.

...

To see both drivers able to push with confidence in these conditions is a good indication of the progress with the underlying pace of the car and a deserved reward for all the hard work from everyone back in Milton Keynes.

...

### Ferrari
Lewis Hamilton was the first to bring out the red flags in final practice, after locking up and running straight into the barriers. Despite a broken front wing, he initially tried to bring the car home before being told to stop by the team.

...

Lewis Hamilton, 4th, 1:32.013
"Although the session didn’t quite end with the result we wanted, it was a solid performance overall. The car felt good throughout. My first lap in Q3 was strong, but it didn’t quite come together on the final run, which cost us a few positions.

...

Charles did a good lap and improved massively through Turns 5 and 6, but with such small gaps between the cars, it was not enough to do better than fifth.

...

### Alpine
It was a mixed bag for Alpine in Qualifying, with both drivers leaving it late to set a lap time in Q2 after their initial runs were interrupted by yellow flags. Franco Colapinto had already had a hairy moment, just catching his car through La Monumental in a very impressive show of skill.

...

“We have a lot to work on and understand after today's result. I was optimistic going into Qualifying as the car felt good all the way through Practice and the pace felt like it was definitely there for the top ten. I just seemed to struggle with grip and the car was sliding around quite a lot and really a handful to drive.

...

We know it will be a challenging race starting from P14 but our pace in Free Practice 2 on high fuel was promising so we have every reason to be confident for tomorrow. We are not sure what the racing will be like at this circuit, it will likely be very tough, but I will give it my all to recover back up into the top ten.”

...

It's definitely a difficult track and we know it does not suit our package too well, so we have really had to take things step by step. I was still learning a lot during Qualifying and we performed very well and I think we maximised everything. I did have a moment at Turn 12, it was very fast and I had to correct it.

...

“It was an exciting Qualifying session at a new track, and you could see all the drivers pushing on the limit. That's what Formula One is all about and is testament to the skill on show today.
Heading into Qualifying, we were trying to get the drivers into a comfortable place with the car, and have it behave and handle the way they need it. We knew we were in a fight to get into Q3 and it would be close with Racing Bulls and Audi.

...

### Audi
Audi were the only team to run the mediums in FP3, although they did not get many laps in thanks to the red flags. On the softs both drivers finished in the top 10, so the team had decent hopes of a strong Qualifying, but they were just pipped in the end and had to settle for P11 and P12.

...

“Looking at tomorrow, I think there is a chance for us to move forward, but it will depend a lot on our pace and how much tyre degradation will impact us. As always, we’ll give our best and see where it takes us.”
Allan McNish, Racing Director
"It was a very tight qualifying session at a circuit on which getting laps together is not easy. Despite this, both Nico and Gabi, as well as the crews, were able to deliver a good performance.
Unfortunately, less than two hundredths of a second was the difference between getting into Q3 or not for Nico: it was a tiny margin, but we were just on the wrong side of that. I think that was the most we could extract for our car, so we can't be too disappointed with that.
Overall, with both cars up there on the edge of the top ten, it was another strong performance by the team, especially in light of the upgrades our rivals have brought in the last few races."

...

### Haas
Unfortunately, that ended his involvement for the day with [too much car damage](https://www.formula1.com/en/latest/article/it-hurts-a-lot-bearman-shouldnt-have-made-that-mistake-as-fp3-crash-rules-him-out-of-madrid-qualifying.26zsvoIU6Y9V5oXdSceZuF) for the team to repair in time for Qualifying.

...

Esteban Ocon made Q3 with relative ease, grabbing 13th on the grid. That is his best Qualifying performance since Japan, showing just how much improvement the team have managed to find through those aero upgrades.
Oliver Bearman, 21st, No time set in Q1
“It’s a shame as the car was quick. It was a tough day yesterday, but we made some changes overnight, and the car was feeling really good in FP3. Unfortunately, I got caught out in Turn 10 on the final lap, and it was a combination of the tyres being a bit old and I had a gust of wind not in my favor.
I shouldn’t have made that mistake – it hurts a lot as the car was strong, but I’m sure there can be some opportunities tomorrow. We have to dust ourselves off and look at the positives, which is that the car was fast and we’ll be giving it everything to do the best we can tomorrow.”

...

“In FP3, we were very happy with the car, the drivers were happy and performing, and we looked competitive. It’s unfortunate that Ollie shunted at the end of FP3, but he’s a great driver and a great guy, and the reason we’re still P7 in the Constructors’ Championship is because in some races, he really delivered.
I have no doubt that will happen again, it’s just sadly happened in a weekend where we have a competitive car – but it happens, it’s racing. We had severe damage and couldn’t get the car ready for Qualifying.
“Esteban’s been having a really good weekend, making progress at a very difficult circuit. His performance in Qualifying was solid, and the fact that it was much hotter in Qualifying, I think we went backwards compared to FP3, but I think it’s pretty obvious why, so that’s something we’re aware of to improve later in the season.

...

(Photo by Bryn Lennon - Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images) MADRID, SPAIN - SEPTEMBER 12: Oliver Bearman of Great Britain and Haas F1 looks at his damaged car MADRID, SPAIN - SEPTEMBER 12: Oliver Bearman of Great Britain and Haas F1 looks at his damaged car after a crash during final practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Spain at

...

### Williams
As such, the Thai driver was up against it in Q1 but pulled a late lap out to scrape into Q2, much to his delight. Sainz could not join him, the Spaniard exiting at the first time of asking in a disappointing afternoon at his home race.

...

On a positive note, this track has been a lot of fun to drive at qualifying pace, and I’m enjoying being so close to the walls and always driving at the limit. It’s been incredible to feel the support of the fans throughout the weekend so far, and it’s a dream come true to be here racing in front of my home crowd.

...

We changed some parts on the car, which thankfully paid off and got us out of Q1, which is an achievement given all the issues we’ve faced. Tomorrow will be a challenge as it’s not an overtaking track, but we’ll do what we can to get a good result.”

...

Well done to Alex, he had almost no laps underneath his belt after a small incident in FP3 but put in a really strong lap to put that car into Q2.
“With Carlos, as you saw there was just milliseconds between the two drivers as there always is. The impeding penalty is the team's responsibility - we didn't warn Carlos of Valtteri behind him and we need to change and improve our systems to make sure we do so in future.

...

### Aston Martin
A further issue was detected in Q1, and the Canadian did not come back out to set a lap time – with the team saying a suspected water pressure issue was the cause. Fernando Alonso did compete, but could not extract enough pace from the car to make Q2.

...

### Cadillac
Cadillac had a solid day in terms of reliability, with both cars completing plenty of laps. Come Qualifying, they did not have the pace to fight with Williams in the end and had to settle for an intra-team battle.

...

“It’s been a tricky weekend for us. You always want to get the most out of the car and today we couldn’t quite get there. We know that we’re lacking in the high speed corners, and it’s a tough track as there are so many blind spots.
I was the first car out in the beginning, but after that was compromised by traffic which was unlucky but sometimes that’s how it goes. We’ll go again tomorrow in the race and hopefully there will be some opportunities.”

...

“Madring is a great addition to the Formula 1 calendar and a big challenge for the drivers. Overall, it was a reasonable qualifying performance today. Checo did well to get the most out of the car.

...

“We are expecting that tomorrow will be a tough, hot and demanding race. It is a track which will test the tyres and concentration. It will be important to stay out of trouble, execute cleanly and make the most of every opportunity.”

...

### Pirelli
"Today’s sessions confirmed the strong performance level of the Soft compound.
Despite the free practice sessions being affected by a lengthy interruption, the teams were able to evaluate different ways of using the C4, with some drivers managing to improve their lap times even within the same run, thanks to track evolution and increasing confidence with the circuit.
For some drivers, a slight drop in performance was observed in the final sector, mainly due to overheating, but overall the red-marked tyre worked extremely well. In fact, compared to the simulations, the quickest qualifying times were around half a second faster.

...

The performance gap between the two compounds is clear, but not significant enough to prevent those with sufficient pace margin from progressing without immediately resorting to the softer option.

...

The C2 is undoubtedly the most consistent compound, and the majority of drivers have preserved both sets for precisely that reason.
"Much will depend, however, on the possible deployment of the Safety Car or Virtual Safety Car, a scenario which, on a street circuit with barriers so close to the track, represents, as we have already seen during the previous sessions, a factor that must be taken very seriously."

        "# F1 teams face big Madring strategy dilemma
## Jon Noble
12 Sep 2026 — 3 min read
Formula 1 isn't really heading for the six-stopper Spanish Grand Prix that George Russell half joked was on the cards after opening practice.
But tyre supplier Pirelli says a combination of factors at F1's newest venue means strategy is going to be particularly tricky to work out.
In fact, the initial prediction following Friday's running is that teams are going to be stuck between a rock and a hard place when working out what is best to do.
The super-long pitlane, which has left the pitstop loss time at around 24 seconds, is a deterrent for tyre changes and means the most logical route should be a one-stopper.
But high levels of thermal degradation of the rubber, and particularly challenging front left graining, means that a two-stop would be sensible.
With no middle ground between those two choices, it is not going to be a case of what is the best strategy to pick. It is about which is the least bad.
**Outside expectations**
F1 teams were left wide-eyed after opening practice when the tyre degradation looked pretty extreme.
A combination of high grip asphalt (highest of the season according to Pirelli), a smooth surface and fast corners has meant cars are sliding a lot – and that triggered some alarming findings during that first session.
As Russell said: "It's often a possibility on new tarmacs that the grip is very high but you're sliding quite aggressively.
"With the deg we had in FP1, a six-stop race would have been the fastest way. FP2 was slightly better and I'm sure the race on Sunday will be better again. But that's the biggest question mark."  
From Pirelli's perspective, there are two issues that drivers and teams are going to have to manage as the Spanish GP weekend continues – and neither is particularly straightforward.
The most complex issue is front left graining, which is being generated because the combination of the smooth surface and high grip means the rubber hits peak stress easily and the surface effectively tears.
Front graining triggers mid-corner understeer and a subsequent drop in performance. It is much harder to manage on the kind of high-speed corners that feature at the Madring than it is at low-speed venues.
Oscar Piastri said after Friday that this element had been the biggest headache from running.
"It's been a nightmare to try and manage the tyres with graining," he said. "It normally gets better through a weekend, but we'll have to wait and see how much better."

...

Pirelli chief engineer Simone Berra reckoned that the drop off here was at a "very high" level – around 0.2-0.3 seconds per lap based on some of the long runs in FP2.
"It was a surprise to have these kinds of values," he said. "They were outside our range of expectations."
While general track evolution and improved set-ups should help reduce that figure by the time the race comes around, the scene is set for the Spanish GP turning into a race where tyre strategy will be critical.
That is what has fuelled all teams apart from Audi electing to keep two hard tyres back after Friday practice – as that could well be the most resilient option for Sunday.
Berra said that the unpredictability thrown up by the front graining and overheating, plus the levels of the degradation, meant that plotting the right path through the race was going to be tough to nail.
"I don't want to exclude any kind of situation," he said. "I think looking from the data, you would think that the teams will go for a two-stop because the degradation is very high.
"But the pitstop loss is 24 seconds, so I'm pretty sure that some teams will try to reach as a target the one-stop race.
"It means we could end up in different situations, with some teams trying the one-stop and other teams trying the two-stops."
Which route is best is unclear right now, and matters are further complicated by how difficult it could be to overtake.

...

Berra added: "If you are in traffic, you lose quite a lot of performance, and you also destroy your tyres because you lose load and you generate high temperatures as you're sliding.
"So, we have different factors that are pushing teams towards different directions.
"It's not easy; in fact, it is pretty complicated."

...

# F1 Spanish Grand Prix 2026 Tyre Strategy
C2 Hard, C3 Medium and C4 Soft make up Pirelli’s range for the Spanish Grand Prix 2026 tyre strategy, and the fastest route to the flag on paper is Medium to Hard, one stop, window Laps 18 to 24. What sits underneath that model is less settled than the number suggests.

...

Spanish Grand Prix 2026 tyre strategy graphic showing five expected pit stop strategies and pit windows for the race at Madrid. _**Expected pit stop strategies for the 2026 Spanish Grand Prix at Madrid, showing five likely race plans and their pit windows. Source: Pirelli race strategy simulations.

...

## **Key Points: Spanish Grand Prix 2026 Tyre Strategy**
* Norris takes pole at Madring’s first ever Grand Prix, 1:31.824, edging Antonelli by 0.011s and Verstappen by 0.14s
* Pirelli confirm C2 Hard, C3 Medium and C4 Soft all raceable.
Medium to Hard rated fastest, window Laps 18 to 24, with an almost identical Medium to Hard to Hard two-stop also live
* Safety Car, VSC and red flag probability all sit at 0% in Pirelli’s data, a blank sheet rather than a low-risk assessment, given FP3 alone was stopped twice by red flags on top of one in FP2

...

* Norris, Antonelli, Verstappen, Russell, Piastri, Colapinto and Lindblad go into Sunday with zero new Soft tyres between them. Hamilton and Leclerc hold the only fresh Softs inside the top six
* Bearman failed to set a qualifying time and starts from the back with the most Soft-heavy allocation on the grid, four new sets in hand

...

## **Setting the Scene**
Norris, Antonelli, Verstappen and Hamilton fill the first two rows, four different teams inside three tenths, and that closeness is happening on a circuit where overtaking has already shown itself to be genuinely hard. Leclerc starts fifth, Russell sixth, Piastri seventh.
Lawson, in the Red Bull seat for a second consecutive weekend while Hadjar continues his recovery, qualified eighth. Colapinto ninth, Lindblad tenth complete the top ten, every one of them on the Soft.

...

This is Madring’s first race weekend and the first Formula 1 Grand Prix held in the Madrid region since Jarama in 1981. There is no prior data from this circuit to lean on, and that absence runs through every part of Sunday’s strategic picture. Qualifying ran in 32 degrees ambient with the track at 53 degrees.

...

## **Friday: Graining Shows Up Early**
All three had started the session on a new Medium before switching to the Soft for their quickest laps. Lindblad, the driver responsible for the stoppage, still ended up fourth fastest. Russell had topped the earlier FP1 session at 1:34.077.
The Medium did the bulk of Friday’s work, 58% of all laps completed on the C3. Bearman got the most out of a single Soft set, 23 laps. Leclerc holds the equivalent benchmark on the Medium, 17 laps on one set.
The Hard barely featured at all, Bortoleto the only driver to run it in FP1, Hulkenberg the only one in FP2, his 1:35.746 standing as the day’s quickest Hard lap. Track temperature peaked at 51 degrees during FP2, air at 32.
> _“We observed graining on both the front and rear left tyres, in some cases quite significant, which contributed to accelerating wear on the cars most prone to sliding.
Differences between the teams are already becoming apparent in terms of who is able to manage the tyres more effectively over a stint.”_**Simone Berra, Pirelli Chief Engineer**
Berra pointed to the Hard as the tyre that matters most this weekend, degradation running higher than Pirelli had expected and the heat forecast to hold through Sunday.
The Medium to Soft gap came in smaller than anticipated too, around half a second rather than the wider figure the pre-event models suggested.
His advice heading into qualifying was blunt: maximise the first flying lap before thermal degradation sets in, and manage traffic carefully, both of which could prove decisive around this circuit.
Spanish Grand Prix 2026 tyre strategy Friday report showing FP1 and FP2 top three times, fastest laps by compound and Pirelli tyre statistics at Madring. _**Pirelli Motorsport Friday report from the 2026 Spanish Grand Prix at Madring, covering FP1 and FP2 times, compound performance and tyre usage.

...

## **Saturday: Norris Takes It, Twice Red-Flagged**
FP3 was built around qualifying simulations and interrupted twice, Hamilton first, into the wall at the final corner, then Bearman at Turn 10.

...

Everyone else stayed on the Soft. Antonelli topped the session at 1:32.797, Leclerc second at 1:32.963, Piastri third at 1:32.986.
Qualifying ran hotter again, 32 degrees air, 53 on track, and the Soft was the tyre almost everybody used to set their time.
Verstappen, Leclerc and Hamilton were the exception, starting Q1 on the Medium to bank a fresh Soft set for the race, a call that shows up directly in Sunday’s tyre allocations. Norris improved on his final lap to take his third pole of the season, 1:31.824.

...

> _“The picture for Sunday remains very open. A one-stop strategy currently appears to be the most natural choice, given the difficulty of overtaking and the time lost in the pit lane.
However, a two-stop strategy could still prove competitive if degradation remains at the levels observed on Friday.”_**Dario Marrafuschi, Pirelli Motorsport Director**
Marrafuschi rates the Medium to Hard and Medium to Hard to Hard combinations as the most likely routes, with the Soft-led versions of each around two seconds slower over race distance.
He also confirmed the detail sitting behind Hamilton and Leclerc’s grid positions, that starting Q1 on the Medium to bank a fresh Soft cost neither driver anything meaningful on pace.
And he flagged the one variable Pirelli’s own numbers can’t account for: a Safety Car or Virtual Safety Car, which he called a factor to take very seriously on a street circuit with barriers this close to the track.
Spanish Grand Prix 2026 tyre strategy Saturday report showing FP3 top three, fastest times by compound and the qualifying top 10 at Madring. **_Pirelli Motorsport Saturday report from the 2026 Spanish Grand Prix at Madring, covering FP3, qualifying and the fastest times by compound.

...

## **Weekend Tyre Picture**
Norris, Antonelli, Russell, Piastri, Colapinto and Lindblad all arrive at Sunday with the identical shape: three used Softs, one new Medium, two new Hards, and nothing fresh in reserve on the red-marked tyre. Verstappen carries the same bank with a used Medium in place of a new one.
Of the front six, Norris, Antonelli, Verstappen and Russell have no new Soft to call on if the race resets. Hamilton and Leclerc are the exceptions, with one fresh set each.
Hamilton and Leclerc are the outliers inside the top six. Their Q1-on-Medium call traded away the fresh Medium but banked them one new Soft each, leaving both with two used Softs, one used Medium and two new Hards.
That new Soft also gives either driver the option to start on it, trading the Medium’s race-length security for the stronger launch off the grid, and if a red flag or Safety Car arrives early, they’ve effectively banked a cheap tyre change on top of the grip advantage.

...

Lawson’s bank is the thinnest at the front on the Hard, four used Softs, one new Medium and just a single new Hard, one fewer than every other front-runner.
Further back, the midfield group, Ocon, Gasly, Tsunoda, Albon, Sainz, Perez and Bottas, all hold a matching one new Soft, three used, one new Medium and two new Hards. Hulkenberg sits a step softer again, four used Softs and only a single new Hard.
Bortoleto is different again: two new Softs, three used, and one new Hard.
Stroll and Alonso hold two of the deepest fresh Soft reserves on the grid, three new sets for Stroll, two for Alonso, both also carrying two new Hards. That’s a tyre bank built for a team running at the back of the field in 2026, not the midfield, with the freedom that comes from having nothing on the line.
Bearman tops the lot. Starting from the back after failing to set a qualifying time, he holds four new Softs and two new Hards, the most Soft-heavy allocation on the grid by some distance. His grid slot undersells the car, too.
Haas sit mid-pack on race pace, ahead of Williams, Aston Martin and Cadillac, which means Bearman is starting at the back of a field his car has no business being stuck in. Haas have nothing to protect from the back, so Bearman can run a strategy nobody else needs to consider.
Spanish Grand Prix 2026 tyre strategy graphic showing the new and used Soft, Medium and Hard tyre sets available to all 22 drivers for the race at Madring. **_Tyres available for the 2026 Spanish Grand Prix at Madring, showing each driver’s remaining new and used Soft, Medium and Hard sets.
Source: Pirelli tyre allocation data. © Coffee Corner Motorsport_**

## **Strategic Impact**
* Norris, Antonelli, Russell, Piastri (P1, P2, P6, P7): matching Medium to Hard shape with a fresh Medium in hand, zero new Softs, race comes down to execution and who protects the rear-left through the opening laps
* Verstappen (P3): same shape as the group above but on a used Medium rather than a new one, a slightly compromised version of the same plan
* Hamilton, Leclerc (P4, P5): the only top-six drivers holding a fresh Soft, giving them the option to start the race on it for a stronger launch rather than saving it, a real point of difference from the rest of the front group
* Lawson (P8): thinnest Hard bank of the front-runners, one new set rather than two, limits his options if the race goes to two stops
* Colapinto, Lindblad (P9, P10): same zero-new-Soft shape as the front six, without the pace to match it

...

* Bearman: four new Softs from the back of the grid, in a Haas that sits mid-pack on race pace, the clearest case on the grid for running something other than the standard one-stop

...

## **A New Track, No History**
One number from earlier in the week has actually been settled. Tuesday’s preview flagged three different pit-loss estimates doing the rounds before a wheel had turned, Pirelli’s own circuit graphic at 25 seconds, McLaren’s technical preview at 19, Alpine’s at 22 and marked as a guess even by their own admission.

...

The weekend’s own Pit Stop Loss Time data has it at 24.2 seconds under green flag, 13 under a Safety Car or VSC, landing right next to Pirelli’s figure and closing the gap that had strategy teams modelling three different scenarios in advance.

## **Strategy Outlook**
**Fastest Plan**
Medium to Hard. Stop window Laps 18 to 24. The route Pirelli rate quickest and the one most of the grid is built for, given how few cars are carrying a fresh Soft.
**Two-Stop Mirror**
Medium to Hard to Hard. Windows Laps 10 to 16 and 31 to 37. The extra pit stop costs time on paper, but running more of the race on fresher tyres claws back most of it, close enough on Pirelli’s numbers that tyre condition rather than lap time decides which one actually wins.

...

**Soft-Led Alternative**
Soft to Hard. Stop window Laps 15 to 21. Brings the pit window forward and trades the Medium’s flexibility for extra grip at the start, useful for anyone looking to make places into Turn 1.
**Soft-Led Two-Stop**
Soft to Hard to Hard. Windows Laps 9 to 15 and 30 to 36. Around two seconds slower than the Medium-based plans on Pirelli’s numbers, and short on the flexibility a driver would want if the first stint doesn’t go to plan.
**Recovery Route: Hard to Medium**
Stop window Laps 36 to 42. The Hail Mary for anyone starting deep, Bearman most obviously. Realistically a strategy that needs a Safety Car or red flag to matter, and this is a circuit where either one is a live possibility even without a single data point to say how likely.
**Ferrari’s Wildcard: Soft Start**
Not one of Pirelli’s five plans, but a real option sitting outside them. Hamilton and Leclerc are free to start the race on their one new Soft rather than banking it, trading the field’s Medium-based security for the stronger launch into Turn 1.

...

## **The Laps 18 to 24 Window**
This is where the front of the grid is supposed to sort itself out.
Norris, Antonelli, Verstappen, Russell and Piastri all have the Medium-to-Hard route available and the same lack of a fresh Soft to fall back on, which means the group at the front is really racing itself on tyre management rather than compound choice.
The driver who protects the rear-left through the opening laps arrives at the window with room to choose the moment. The driver who doesn’t gets forced in early, and on a track this hard to pass on, an early stop into clear traffic is expensive in a way it wouldn’t be somewhere with more overtaking chances.
A red flag or Safety Car landing inside that window collapses it for everyone still out, and hands an unplanned reset to whoever is already offset, Lawson on his thinner Hard bank, or Bearman running his own race entirely from the back. Nobody has the data to say how likely that is here.
Given what practice has already shown, that is a gap worth planning for rather than dismissing.

## **What Will Decide the Race**
* The graining Pirelli logged on Friday, and whether it’s a front-axle problem the field can manage or a rear-left one that forces early stops regardless of the model
* Norris defending pole through the Laps 18 to 24 window against four cars carrying an almost identical tyre allocation
* A red flag or Safety Car arriving at all, on data that offers no real steer either way
* Hamilton and Leclerc’s single fresh Soft each, and whether that spare set turns into the difference-maker it looks like on paper
* Bearman’s four new Softs from the back, and whether Madring hands him the reset needed to turn them into points

## **Coffee Corner Take**
Zero percent means one thing here. Pirelli have nothing to go on. Two red flags in one practice session, barriers that took an age to clear each time, and a Safety Car figure that reads exactly the same as if none of that had happened at all.

...

Sunday comes down to who manages the rear-left best through the first stint, on top of whatever those small differences are worth. It’s execution first, tyre bank second.
Hamilton and Leclerc’s decision to sacrifice track position risk in Q1 for a spare Soft looks like the kind of call that only pays off if the race actually asks the question. If it stays a clean one-stop, it’s a nice-to-have that never gets used.

...

Bearman is a driver with options out of place. No lap time, back of the grid, and the only driver on the sheet carrying four fresh Softs. That’s deliberate. Haas sit mid-pack on race pace, well clear of Williams, Aston Martin and Cadillac, so the car doesn’t belong at the back either."

[George Russell](https://www.motorsport.com/driver/george-russell/21167/) was the fastest long-run driver with a lot of fuel on board.
His closest challenger was Red Bull’s [Max Verstappen](https://www.motorsport.com/driver/max-verstappen/17529/) over Friday’s practice

...

The Dutchman was just 0.13 seconds per lap slower after adjusting for different tyre compounds and stint lengths.
World championship leader Kimi Antonelli was the third-fastest long-run driver, although he was 0.55s per lap behind Russell.
[Ferrari](https://www.motorsport.com/team/ferrari/3/) and [McLaren](https://www.motorsport.com/team/mclaren/10/) were disappointing

...

Both Ferraris were around nine tenths of a second per lap slower than [Mercedes](https://www.motorsport.com/team/mercedes/5/) , while
Oscar Piastri's long run was even 1.51s per lap slower.
Team-mate [Lando Norris](https://www.motorsport.com/driver/lando-norris/289316/) was unable to complete any long runs due to technical

...

## Has Mercedes not shown everything yet?
On race Sunday, however, the Silver Arrows were ultimately eight tenths per lap faster than both teams.
Mercedes therefore traditionally appears to show less on Fridays than the competition, which could be a bad omen for the rest of the weekend. However, caution is also required, as the track in Madrid is new. Larger setup changes can therefore be expected for Saturday.
The competition also appears to be closer over a single lap. If the fastest sector times of each driver are added together, [Charles Leclerc](https://www.motorsport.com/driver/charles-leclerc/109611/) could theoretically have set the fastest lap with a 1:33.478.
Of the top six drivers, however, only [Arvid Lindblad](https://www.motorsport.com/driver/arvid-lindblad/953482/) was able to combine all of his best sector times into a single lap.

...

## Does Mercedes have better battery management?
Mercedes was already able to set the fastest time in the third sector during the qualifying simulations, but with a lot of fuel on board, the team can apparently extend that advantage even further.
Ferrari appear to be off the pace of Mercedes

...

## Midfield: Where did Haas suddenly come from?
Team-mate [Yuki Tsunoda](https://www.motorsport.com/driver/yuki-tsunoda/828523/) was also running a different programme and completed his qualifying and race simulations in a single stint, probably with a low fuel load.
That meant Haas actually recorded the best long-run pace in the midfield. [Esteban Ocon](https://www.motorsport.com/driver/esteban-ocon/19624/) was just 0.92s per lap behind Mercedes' Russell during his stint, putting the Frenchman practically on Ferrari's level.
[Alpine](https://www.motorsport.com/team/alpine/24858/) (+1.60), [Audi](https://www.motorsport.com/team/audi/49022/) (+2.20), [Williams](https://www.motorsport.com/team/williams/13/) (+2.58), Cadillac (+4.00) and Aston Martin (+4.33) followed behind, with some considerable gaps.

...

## “Six stops”: How high is tyre degradation in Madrid?
The performance of some teams was not the only surprise on Friday. The behaviour of the tyres was also unexpected. As a street circuit with what is essentially a smooth asphalt surface, high tyre degradation was not initially expected. However, that may now be changing.
“At the beginning it was tricky because the track has so much grip, even though it is completely new asphalt,” Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff explained to Sky. “And interestingly, we have the opposite problem to what we expected. We can't quite get the tyre up to temperature.

...

“We've never seen that before,” said Wolff. “Our strategy chief said six stops. But I think in the end it will be one stop.”

...

...

“The grip of the asphalt is really good, so we will most likely have less degradation than expected.”
The further course of the weekend in Madrid will show who ultimately gets their prediction right.

  url=f'https://api.jolpi.ca/ergast/f1/2026/{endpoint}.json?limit=100&offset={off}'

  for r in races:

   if found: found[field].extend(r[field])
   else: allr.append(r)
  if off+100>=int(d['MRData']['total']):break
 json.dump(allr,open(f'/workspace/data/{endpoint}_races.json','w'),indent=2)

{"command":"cat > /workspace/analyze.py <<'PY'
import json, collections, statistics, math
rr=json.load(open('/workspace/data/results_races.json'))
qq=json.load(open('/workspace/data/qualifying_races.json'))
print('RACE RESULTS')
for r in rr:

 print(' '.join(f"{x['Driver'].get('code','?')}:{x['positionText']}({x['status']})" for x in r['Results']))
print('\nQUALI')
for r in qq:
 print(r['round'],r['raceName'],' '.join(f"{x['Driver'].get('code','?')}:{x['position']}" for x in sorted(r['QualifyingResults'],key=lambda z:int(z['position']))))

 res=[]; qs=[]

  x=next((x for x in r['Results'] if x['Driver'].get('code')==c),None)
  if x: res.append((int(r['round']),x['positionText'],x['status'],int(x['position'])))
 for r in qq:
  x=next((x for x in r['QualifyingResults'] if x['Driver'].get('code')==c),None)
  if x: qs.append((int(r['round']),int(x['position'])))
 finish=[p for _,pt,s,p in res if pt.isdigit()]
 nonfin=[z for z in res if not z[1].isdigit()]

PY
python /workspace/analyze.py > /workspace/summary.txt

import numpy as np
p={'ANT':.39,'NOR':.34,'VER':.115,'HAM':.065,'RUS':.04,'LEC':.03,'PIA':.015,'LAW':.003,'LIN':.001,'COL':.0005,'HUL':.0003,'BOR':.0002,'OCO':.00015,'GAS':.00015}
ks=list(p); w=np.array(list(p.values()));w=w/w.sum(); n=1000000;rng=np.random.default_rng(1); cnt=np.zeros(len(w));wins=np.zeros(len(w))
chunk=100000
for z in range(0,n,chunk):
 t=rng.exponential(1/w,(min(chunk,n-z),len(w)))
 ind=np.argpartition(t,3,axis=1)[:,:3]
 cnt += (ind[:,:,None]==np.arange(len(w))).sum(axis=(0,1))
 wins += (np.argmin(t,axis=1)[:,None]==np.arange(len(w))).sum(axis=0)
print('sum',sum(cnt)/n)
for k,wi,wn,pod in zip(ks,w,wins/n,cnt/n): print(k,round(wi,4),round(wn,4),round(pod,4))
PY
